headline: High: shared filesystem and broad shell/network access make prompt injection, leakage, and cascading errors plausible by default.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: OpenMetadata can expose content through APIs, events, webhooks, and an MCP server, while Plandex reads/writes a project directory and stdin/stdout. That creates a plausible bridge where OpenMetadata output can be fed into Plandex as trusted text. The pair lacks documented provenance controls, so interaction risk is real even without a direct exploit proof.
conditions: IF OpenMetadata outputs are copied into Plandex prompts or plan files without provenance tags, injection becomes actionable.
IF Plandex auto-applies instructions derived from OpenMetadata text, malicious content can steer actions.
mitigations: Disable auto-apply in Plandex for any OpenMetadata-derived content.
Add a manual review step before copying catalog text into plans.
Prefix imported OpenMetadata text as untrusted data, not instructions.
Restrict OpenMetadata webhooks/events from reaching Plandex inputs.
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging between the two tools.

B_data_leakage.rationale: OpenMetadata touches governance, lineage, semantics, and memory/trust data, while Plandex reads and writes files and sends context to a model provider or Plandex Cloud. If OpenMetadata-managed metadata is placed in the shared project directory, Plandex can ingest and transmit it externally. The profiles do not show isolation between their file surfaces, so leakage is plausible in default use.
conditions: IF OpenMetadata metadata or governance notes are stored in Plandex's project directory, Plandex can read them.
IF Plandex sends that context to a model provider or cloud backend, the data leaves the local workspace.
mitigations: Keep OpenMetadata exports out of Plandex project directories.
Use a redaction pass before any Plandex prompt includes catalog content.
Run Plandex against synthetic or scrubbed metadata only.
Limit Plandex network egress during shared workflows.
requires-engineering: separate workspaces and access controls for the two agents.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: OpenMetadata supports multiple instances and MCP/API/event/webhook interaction, while Plandex has broad filesystem write, shell, subprocess, and git-state modification plus shared backend state. If both operate on the same repo or workspace, concurrent writes and git changes can collide without a locking primitive being documented. Uncertainty about orchestration increases severity rather than lowering it.
conditions: IF both agents target the same directory or git repository, write conflicts can occur.
IF OpenMetadata-driven automation and Plandex both mutate shared files without locks, state corruption is possible.
mitigations: Assign separate working directories to each agent.
Pause one agent before the other writes to the repo.
Avoid concurrent git operations during shared runs.
Use a manual merge/review step after each agent's changes.
requires-engineering: add file and git locking around shared resources.

D_cascading_error.rationale: OpenMetadata can emit governance and lineage outputs that Plandex may ingest as planning context, and Plandex can then act through shell, subprocess, and git operations. That makes a mistaken catalog fact capable of propagating into code or repo changes. Plandex has review-then-apply safeguards, so this is not high, but the default pathway still exists.
conditions: IF Plandex treats OpenMetadata output as authoritative planning input, errors can cascade into actions.
IF review is bypassed or auto-apply is enabled, incorrect metadata can become repo changes.
mitigations: Require verification of OpenMetadata facts before planning.
Keep Plandex in review-then-apply mode.
Block auto-apply for any OpenMetadata-derived task.
Add a second human check for repo-affecting actions.
requires-engineering: implement source-citation checks before execution.

E_compliance.rationale: OpenMetadata touches governance and memory/trust data, while Plandex handles source code and model-provider secrets. The profiles do not show a residency or certification mismatch, so a compliance breach is not established. The only concrete concern is that sensitive metadata could be routed into Plandex's external model-provider path if operators mix datasets.
conditions: IF regulated metadata is copied into Plandex prompts, it may be sent to a third-party model provider.
IF the deployment has residency or retention constraints not reflected in the profiles, a policy mismatch can occur.
mitigations: Exclude regulated data from Plandex prompts.
Use a local or approved model backend only.
Review retention settings before shared runs.
Document the data classes allowed in each tool.
requires-engineering: enforce residency and retention policy gates.
